The End of Print:
The Graphic Design of David Carson

The 1995 monograph on David Carson by Lewis Blackwell, with an introduction by David Byrne, whose cover mixes blurred, mirrored, and substituted letters over photo fragments.

Source
Design Reviewed: The End of Print, Laurence King, 1995
Creator
David Carson
Made
1995 (Design Reviewed; Chronicle Books edition, ISBN 0-8118-1199-9, per Wikipedia)
Style
Grunge typography (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Chaotic, intuitive, layered
Evidence
Inspected Design Reviewed’s scan of the Laurence King edition cover (1600 × 1600) in a scratchpad copy. The interior was not seen. Design Reviewed’s page returned 403 to scripts and was read through WebFetch. Not stored.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

Design Reviewed lists the book as published by Laurence King in 1995, designed by David Carson, 245 × 285 mm. Design Reviewed.

Wikipedia lists the US edition as Chronicle Books, 1995, ISBN 0-8118-1199-9. Wikipedia).

An Internet Archive lending copy is catalogued as “The end of print: the graphic design of David Carson” by Lewis Blackwell. Internet Archive.

Observed

  • The cover is divided into pale yellow, deep blue, and orange panels, with photo fragments of a machine part and an astronomical chart labelled “Mercury” and “Venus”.
  • “THE END OF PRINT:” mixes letters from different serif and blackletter-like faces; several letters are blurred, doubled, or mirrored, and a thin rule runs under the line.
  • “DATUM” is printed upside down in a heavy sans-serif beside a vertical rule.
  • “THE GRAPHIC DESIGN OF DAVID CARSON” uses substituted and reversed letters: a numeral 1 for I, a reversed E, and a mirrored S in “CARSON”.
  • “CARSON” is very large white serif capitals over a blue photograph; the author lines are a spaced sans-serif and an italic serif.

Why it belongs

The cover is milder than the Ray Gun pages but carries the core traits: mixed faces within one word, damaged or mirrored letters, and type laid over photographic fragments.

Borrow

Replace a few letters in a title with glyphs from other faces, or mirror them, and keep the word readable.

Blur or double one or two letters in a display line instead of the whole line.
